questions.q: Why does the lesson say three different stakeholders can honestly disagree about whether a governance program is succeeding?
options: Because they're measuring different things — stewards look at data quality, sponsors look at approval speed, executives look at trust in reported numbers
Because one of them is always lying
Because only executives are allowed to define success
Because governance metrics are randomly generated
questions.explain: Stewards, business sponsors, and executives each judge success by a different lens, and the lesson says none of these views alone is complete.

questions.q: What is the difference between a compliance metric and an outcome metric, per this lesson?
options: Compliance measures whether people did what a policy required; outcome measures whether doing it actually produced the intended result
They are two names for the same thing
Compliance metrics are always more accurate than outcome metrics
Outcome metrics are easier to measure than compliance metrics
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly defines compliance as 'did people do the thing' and outcome as 'did it actually help' — and notes outcomes are harder to measure.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a 95% policy acknowledgment rate actually tell you?
options: That people clicked "I agree" — nothing about whether their behavior actually changed
That the policy definitely improved data quality
That the governance program has succeeded
That no further measurement is needed
questions.explain: The lesson uses this exact example to illustrate that a compliance metric alone proves nothing about outcomes.

questions.q: The lesson warns that a program hitting every metric target can still be failing. Why?
options: The targets may have been set too low to matter, or a team may have learned to game the metric instead of improving the real behavior
Metric targets are always set correctly, so this can't actually happen
Hitting every target always means true success
Dashboards are incapable of showing all-green status
questions.explain: The lesson gives these two specific failure modes: targets set too low, and metrics being gamed rather than the underlying behavior improving.

questions.q: Why might a program that misses several targets in its first two quarters still be on a legitimate path to success?
options: Because real change often takes longer than one quarter to show up in lagging metrics
Because missed targets should always be ignored
Because quarterly measurement is never meaningful
Because targets are only symbolic and never matter
questions.explain: The lesson explains that lagging metrics can take multiple quarters to reflect real underlying change.
